Let $F:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be locally Lipschitz, and let $R=\prod_{i=1}^m[a_i,b_i]\subset U$ with finite $a_i<b_i$. The rectangle is **reaction-inward** if, for every $i$, $F_i(z)\ge0$ on the lower face $z_i=a_i$ and $F_i(z)\le0$ on the upper face $z_i=b_i$, with all other coordinates in their intervals. It is **reaction-invariant** if the solution map $\Phi_F^t$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ on $R$ and $\Phi_F^t(R)\subseteq R$ for every $t\ge0$.

For a rectangle with $a_i=0$ for all $i$, the lower-face condition is exactly quasi-positivity from [[def-reaction-vector-field-and-quasipositivity]]. The upper-face condition is independent and must be checked separately. The inward-sign condition is a hypothesis, not by definition an invariance theorem.

Let $F:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be the reaction vector field of [[def-reaction-vector-field-and-quasipositivity]], and let $R\subset U$ be a state set. A vector $c\in[0,\infty)^m$ is a **stoichiometric conservation vector on $R$** if $c^TF(z)=0$ for every $z\in R$. It is a **stoichiometric dissipation vector on $R$** if $c^TF(z)\le0$ for every $z\in R$. The corresponding pointwise mass is $c^Tz$.

For a measurable domain $\Omega$, the continuous total mass is $\mathcal M_c(u)=\int_\Omega c^Tu(x)\,dx$. For any finite index set $I$ with assigned positive weights $m_i$, the discrete total mass of states $U_i\in\mathbb R^m$ is $\mathcal M_{c,h}(U)=\sum_{i\in I}m_ic^TU_i$. The weights and index set are part of the discrete model. Conservation and dissipation always refer to these stated functionals and the stated state set; no claim is made for a different weight vector or for reactions outside $R$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim: Let $z(t)$ be the unique local solution from [F3] and let $p(t)$ be the coordinatewise projection of $z(t)$ onto $R$. While $z(t)\in R_\delta$, define $V(t)=\sum_i((a_i-z_i(t))_+^2+(z_i(t)-b_i)_+^2)$, where $x_+=\max(x,0)$. The squared positive-part function is continuously differentiable. If $z_i<a_i$, then $p_i=a_i$ and [F1], [A1] give $F_i(z)\ge F_i(p)-L\|z-p\|\ge-L\|z-p\|$; if $z_i>b_i$, then $p_i=b_i$ and $F_i(z)\le F_i(p)+L\|z-p\|\le L\|z-p\|$. Differentiating the active terms of $V$ therefore yields $V'(t)\le C_m L V(t)$ for a finite constant $C_m$ depending only on $m$.

Since $V(0)=0$, integrating $V'(t)\le C_mLV(t)$ gives $0\le V(t)\le C_mL\int_0^tV(s)\,ds$ on any initial interval where $z$ remains in $R_\delta$. Apply Gronwall's inequality [F5] to obtain $V(t)=0$. Thus $z(t)$ cannot leave $R$ on its local interval of existence.

The field is bounded by $M_F$ on $R$ by [A1]. If a maximal solution interval had a finite right endpoint $T_*$, then $\|z(t)-z(s)\|\le M_F|t-s|$ for $s,t<T_*$, so $z(t)$ has a limit $z_*\in R$ as $t\uparrow T_*$. The open domain contains $z_*$, so [F3] gives a solution starting at $(T_*,z_*)$; local uniqueness in [F3] joins it to the original solution, contradicting maximality [F4]. Hence the solution exists for every $t\ge0$, and step 2.1 keeps it in $R$.

Along the solution, $\frac d{dt}(c^Tz(t))=c^TF(z(t))$. By [F2] this derivative is zero in the conservation case and nonpositive in the dissipation case. Integrating over $[0,t]$ proves the corresponding mass conclusion.

derivations.claim: Fix coordinate $i$ and keep the other coordinates of $z$ fixed. Let $z^-$ replace $z_i$ by $a_i$. By [F1], $F_i(z^-)\ge0$; hence [A1] gives $F_i(z)\ge-L_i(z_i-a_i)$. Similarly, let $z^+$ replace $z_i$ by $b_i$. Then [F1] and [A1] give $F_i(z)\le L_i(b_i-z_i)$.

If $L_i>0$, the lower estimate yields $z_i+\tau F_i(z)-a_i\ge(1-\tau L_i)(z_i-a_i)\ge0$, and the upper estimate yields $b_i-z_i-\tau F_i(z)\ge(1-\tau L_i)(b_i-z_i)\ge0$. If $L_i=0$, [A1] makes $F_i$ independent of $z_i$ on the coordinate interval; its lower and upper face signs force $F_i(z)=0$. Thus every coordinate of $z^+$ lies in its interval.
The Euler formula gives $c^Tz^+=c^Tz+\tau c^TF(z)$. Apply [F2] to get equality for a conservation vector and the claimed inequality for a dissipation vector.

$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If Omega has the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, then $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$, with faces counted once off E. All integrals are finite. In a specified finite gluing, the two fluxes on every shared face cancel.

Under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]], a finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of a nonempty bounded open $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, consists of compact faces $S_1,\ldots,S_q$ covering its boundary, each a compact Borel subset of a regular $C^1$ hypersurface patch, and a compact edge set $E\subset\partial\Omega$. Require $S_j\cap E$ to have surface measure zero in each face, using [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]]. E contains the boundaries of the faces relative to their patches and every overlap $S_i\cap S_j$, i different from j. At every point outside E the domain boundary is locally a single $C^1$ graph with Omega on one side. Each face carries this actual outward unit normal off E. Values assigned to the normal on E do not affect its integral.

For a specified finite gluing also list the open pieces with disjoint interiors, the shared faces, and their opposite outward normals. Require the pieces to cover the final domain up to their boundary faces, and the exposed faces to give its specified presentation. Internal faces are counted twice before cancellation, once from each side. The phrase piecewise smooth by itself supplies none of this data.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Since $u_t$ is continuous on the compact cylinder, the time difference quotient of $c^Tu$ is the time average of $c^Tu_t$ by [F4], and uniform continuity makes it converge uniformly to $c^Tu_t$. Each stated domain has finite volume, so integrating this uniform convergence proves $\frac d{dt}\int_\Omega c^Tu=\int_\Omega c^Tu_t$.

In the box branch, substitute [F1] into step 1.1. The diffusion contribution is $\sum_i c_id_i\int_\Omega\Delta u_i\,dx$. For each coordinate $j$, [F3] permits integration in $x_j$ first, and [F4] gives $\int_0^{L_j}\partial_{jj}u_i\,dx_j=\partial_ju_i|_{x_j=L_j}-\partial_ju_i|_{x_j=0}$. This difference is zero for matching periodic traces and is zero for homogeneous Neumann data. Summing over components and coordinates makes the total diffusion contribution vanish.

In the specified piecewise $C^1$ branch, each vector field $
abla u_i$ is $C^1$ on the closure. Apply [F5] using the domain presentation [F6] and the axiom assumption [F7]: $\int_\Omega\Delta u_i\,dx=\sum_j\int_{S_j}
abla u_i\cdot
u_j\,dS$. By [A1], the integrand is zero on every face outside its surface-null edge set; hence every face integral vanishes. Thus the diffusion contribution to step 1.1 is also zero in this branch.

In either branch, after the diffusion term vanishes, the remaining derivative is $\int_\Omega c^TF(u(x,t))\,dx$. By [F2] its integrand is identically zero in the conservation case and nonpositive in the dissipation case. Integrating proves the claimed mass derivative and monotonicity.

Fix $d\ge1$, side lengths $L_j>0$, and integers $N_j\ge3$. Put $h_j=L_j/N_j$, $\mathbb T_L^d=\prod_{j=1}^d(\mathbb R/L_j\mathbb Z)$, and $G_h=\prod_{j=1}^d(\mathbb Z/N_j\mathbb Z)$. Grid nodes are $x_i=((i_j+\tfrac12)h_j)_{j=1}^d$ modulo the side lengths, grid indices wrap modulo $N_j$, and $P_hu=(u(x_i))_{i\in G_h}$ denotes sampling. The cell volume is $m_h=\prod_jh_j$. The positive periodic heat stencil is the unit-diffusivity specialization of the periodic operator in [[def-parabolic-theta-finite-difference-scheme]]:
$$
(A_h^{\rm per}v)_i=\sum_{j=1}^d\frac{2v_i-v_{i+e_j}-v_{i-e_j}}{h_j^2}.
$$
For $s$ species with diffusivities $d_r\ge0$, the reaction-diffusion grid generator acts on species $r$ by $-d_rA_h^{\rm per}$. Each grid node has weight $m_h=\prod_jh_j$; the stencil has zero row and column sums, so each species' weighted sum is conserved by diffusion. Its matrix representation satisfies $L_h=m_hA_h^{\rm per}$, with symmetric $L_h$, nonpositive off-diagonal entries and $L_h\mathbf1=0$.

The sign convention is that $A_h^{\rm per}$ is nonnegative and $-d_rA_h^{\rm per}$ generates diffusion. The exact eigenvalues of the positive stencil are supplied by [[lem-periodic-heat-difference-amplification-symbol]]. This grid is the only spatial discretization used in the periodic error theorem; no mesh-uniform claim for general finite-volume meshes is made there.

Under the hypotheses of [[thm-taylor-schlomilch-roche-remainder]], there are points $\xi_L,\xi_C$ between $a$ and $x$ such that
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_L)}{\iota((n+1)!)}(x-a)^{n+1}$$
and

The positive periodic heat stencil is the unit-diffusivity specialization of the periodic operator in [[def-parabolic-theta-finite-difference-scheme]]:
$$
(A_h^{\rm per}v)_i=\sum_{j=1}^d\frac{2v_i-v_{i+e_j}-v_{i-e_j}}{h_j^2}.
$$
For $s$ species with diffusivities $d_r\ge0$, the reaction-diffusion grid generator acts on species $r$ by $-d_rA_h^{\rm per}$. Each grid node has weight $m_h=\prod_jh_j$; the stencil has zero row and column sums, so each species' weighted sum is conserved by diffusion. Its matrix representation satisfies $L_h=m_hA_h^{\rm per}$, with symmetric $L_h$, nonpositive off-diagonal entries and $L_h\mathbf1=0$.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be locally Lipschitz. Write $F_i$ for its $i$th component. The autonomous reaction equation is $z'(t)=F(z(t))$. The field is **quasi-positive** on $U\cap[0,\infty)^m$ if, for every $i$ and every $z\in U\cap[0,\infty)^m$ with $z_i=0$, one has $F_i(z)\ge0$. This condition concerns only the coordinate faces of the nonnegative orthant.

For a rectangle $R=\prod_{i=1}^m[a_i,b_i]\subset U$ with $a_i<b_i$, the field is **inward-pointing on $R$** if $F_i(z)\ge0$ whenever $z\in R$ and $z_i=a_i$, and $F_i(z)\le0$ whenever $z\in R$ and $z_i=b_i$. If $a_i=0$ for every $i$, quasi-positivity supplies the lower-face half of this condition, but the upper-face inequalities remain separate hypotheses. Neither boundary condition by itself asserts that a numerical update preserves $R$.

For smoothness-dependent results below, $F\in C^4(U,\mathbb R^m)$ will be stated explicitly. No smoothness beyond local Lipschitz continuity is built into this definition.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

derivations.claim: Let $w$ be a twice differentiable scalar function on a coordinate lift with bounded $w''$. By [F6], $w'$ is continuous; hence $s\mapsto w'(x+s)-w'(x-s)$ is continuous and integrable on $[0,h]$ by [F4]. Apply [F3] to the differentiable function $s\mapsto w(x+s)+w(x-s)-2w(x)$, whose endpoint derivatives are the corresponding one-sided restrictions. This gives $$w(x+h)-2w(x)+w(x-h)=\int_0^h\bigl(w'(x+s)-w'(x-s)\bigr)\,ds.$$ For $s>0$, [F5] applied to $w'$ on $[x-s,x+s]$ gives $|w'(x+s)-w'(x-s)|\le2s\|w''\|_\infty$; at $s=0$ this also holds. Integrating yields $|w(x+h)-2w(x)+w(x-h)|\le h^2\|w''\|_\infty$. Thus the centered second difference divided by $h^2$ has the same mesh-independent bound. Only the continuous first derivative was integrated; integrability or continuity of $w''$ is not assumed.

Fix a component $i$ and a spatial direction $j$. The chain rule first gives $\partial_j(F_i(u))=\sum_k\partial_kF_i(u)\,\partial_ju_k$. Applying the product rule to each summand and the chain rule to $\partial_kF_i(u)$ gives $$\partial_{jj}(F_i(u))=\sum_k\partial_kF_i(u)\,\partial_{jj}u_k+\sum_{k,\ell}\partial_{k\ell}F_i(u)(\partial_ju_k)(\partial_ju_\ell).$$ These are pointwise identities under the stated second-order spatial differentiability of $u$ and $F\in C^2$ near its range. To express the bound using only the quantities listed in the Statement, let $w_k=\sup_R z_k-\inf_R z_k$ and $H_{kj}=\|\partial_{jj}u_k\|_\infty$. For $g(s)=u_k(x+se_j,t)$ on the periodic lift, $g'$ is continuous by [F6], and $r\mapsto g'(r)-g'(0)$ is integrable on $[0,s]$ by [F4]. Apply [F3] to $r\mapsto g(r)-g(0)-rg'(0)$ to get $g(s)-g(0)-sg'(0)=\int_0^s(g'(r)-g'(0))\,dr$. By [F5] on $g'$, $|g'(r)-g'(0)|\le rH_{kj}$ for $0\le r\le s$. The remainder is therefore bounded by $s^2H_{kj}/2$. Since $|g(s)-g(0)|\le w_k$, this yields, for every $s>0$, $$s|\partial_ju_k(x,t)|\le w_k+\frac{s^2}{2}H_{kj}.$$ If $w_kH_{kj}>0$, choose $s=\sqrt{2w_k/H_{kj}}$ to obtain $|\partial_ju_k|\le\sqrt{2w_kH_{kj}}$. If $H_{kj}=0$, the same inequality for every $s$ gives $\partial_ju_k=0$; if $w_k=0$, the component is constant and the same conclusion holds. Therefore the displayed chain-rule terms are uniformly bounded in terms of $R$, $D^2u$, $DF$, and $D^2F$, as asserted.

In each component, $\mathcal A_hF_h(P_hu)$ is a finite sum of $d_i$ times the centered second differences of $F_i\circ u$, while $DF(P_hu)\mathcal A_hP_hu$ is the finite sum of $\partial_kF_i(u)d_k$ times the centered second differences of $u_k$. Step 1.1 bounds each difference uniformly, and step 2.1 bounds every coefficient. There are only $d m^2$ terms and $D$ is fixed, so their sum is bounded by a constant independent of all $h_j$.

On the finite periodic rectangular $d$-grid of [[def-parabolic-theta-finite-difference-scheme]], let $\ell_j\in\{0,\ldots,N_j-1\}$ and
$$
\phi_\ell(i)=\exp\left(2\pi\mathrm i\sum_{j=1}^d\frac{\ell_ji_j}{N_j}\right).
$$
Then $\phi_\ell$ is an eigenvector of $A_h^{\rm per}$ with eigenvalue
$$
\lambda_\ell=4\sum_{j=1}^d\frac{\kappa_j}{h_j^2}\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi\ell_j}{N_j}\right)\ge0.
$$
For zero source, the $\theta$ update multiplies this mode at each step by

g_\theta(\ell)=\frac{1-(1-\theta)\Delta t\lambda_\ell}{1+\theta\Delta t\lambda_\ell}.
$$
The displayed modes form a basis of the complexified grid space, so this factor describes the full periodic update.

derivations.claim: Write $u=y_*+\varepsilon w$. Differentiability of $F$ gives $F(y_*+\varepsilon w)=F(y_*)+\varepsilon Jw+o(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon Jw+o(\varepsilon)$, so the linearized equation is $w_t=D\Delta w+Jw$. For a continuous torus mode $w(t,x)=a(t)e^{2\pi i\sum_jk_jx_j/L_j}$, direct differentiation gives $\Delta w=-\lambda_kw$ and hence $a'=(J-\lambda_kD)a$.

For every $\lambda\ge0$, $\operatorname{tr}(J-\lambda D)=\operatorname{tr}J-\lambda(d_1+d_2)<0$. Expanding the $2\times2$ determinant gives $\det(J-\lambda D)=(J_{11}-\lambda d_1)(J_{22}-\lambda d_2)-J_{12}J_{21}=d_1d_2\lambda^2-\beta_T\lambda+\det J=q(\lambda)$.

For the grid, insert a Fourier vector from [F3] into the linearized finite system. By [F2] its diffusion part multiplies that mode by $-D\lambda_{h,\ell}$; the reaction Jacobian acts on the species coordinate by $J$. Therefore the mode coefficient satisfies $a'=(J-\lambda_{h,\ell}D)a$. The basis assertion in [F3] ensures these are the actual grid mode matrices.

The characteristic polynomial of a real $2\times2$ matrix $A$ is $\mu^2-\operatorname{tr}(A)\mu+\det(A)$. If $\operatorname{tr}(A)<0$ and $\det(A)<0$, its discriminant $\operatorname{tr}(A)^2-4\det(A)$ is positive and the real roots have negative product, so one is positive. If $\operatorname{tr}(A)<0$ and $\det(A)>0$, real roots have negative sum and positive product, so both are negative; nonreal roots are conjugate with real part $\operatorname{tr}(A)/2<0$. If the determinant is zero, one eigenvalue is zero and the other is the trace, which is negative. Applying these alternatives to $A=J-\lambda D$ proves the mode tests in the Statement.

Since $d_1d_2>0$ and $\det J>0$, the upward-opening quadratic $q$ is negative at some $\lambda\ge0$ exactly when its minimum occurs at a positive point and its discriminant is strictly positive. Its minimizer is $\beta_T/(2d_1d_2)$, so the first condition is $\beta_T>0$; its discriminant is $\beta_T^2-4d_1d_2\det J$, so the second condition is the strict inequality in the Statement. Under these conditions both roots are positive because their sum is $\beta_T/(d_1d_2)>0$ and product is $\det J/(d_1d_2)>0$, and factorization gives $q<0$ precisely between them. The mode tests from step 2.2 then prove the continuous-spectrum and finite-grid criteria without replacing either actual spectrum by all real wavenumbers.

$$
c_{KL}=\sum_{F=K|L}T_F,
$$

If more than one face separates a cell pair, summing their conductances gives the same cell-balance flux as retaining the faces separately. Define the symmetric matrix $L_h$ by $(L_h)_{KK}=\sum_{L\ne K}c_{KL}$ and $(L_h)_{KL}=-c_{KL}$ for $K\ne L$.

|K|(U_{K,r})'=d_r\sum_{L:c_{KL}>0}c_{KL}(U_{L,r}-U_{K,r}).
$$
The equality is the usual shared-face TPFA balance with outward flux $T_F(U_{K,r}-U_{L,r})$ and no boundary flux. For a finite real square matrix $A$, define

$$e^{tA}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^kA^k}{k!}.$$

This series converges absolutely and uniformly for $t$ in every bounded interval. It is differentiable with $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=Ae^{tA}=e^{tA}A$ and $e^{0A}=I$. If finite square matrices $A$ and $B$ commute, then $e^Ae^B=e^{A+B}$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and

Let $F:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be the reaction vector field of [[def-reaction-vector-field-and-quasipositivity]], and let $R\subset U$ be a state set. A vector $c\in[0,\infty)^m$ is a **stoichiometric conservation vector on $R$** if $c^TF(z)=0$ for every $z\in R$. It is a **stoichiometric dissipation vector on $R$** if $c^TF(z)\le0$ for every $z\in R$. The corresponding pointwise mass is $c^Tz$.

For a measurable domain $\Omega$, the continuous total mass is $\mathcal M_c(u)=\int_\Omega c^Tu(x)\,dx$. The weights and index set are part of the discrete model. Conservation and dissipation always refer to these stated functionals and the stated state set; no claim is made for a different weight vector or for reactions outside $R$.

Let $F\in C^1$ and let $y_*\in\mathbb R^2$ be a homogeneous equilibrium, $F(y_*)=0$. Set $J=DF(y_*)=(J_{ij})$, assume $\operatorname{tr}J<0$ and $\det J>0$, and let $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,d_2)$ with $d_1,d_2>0$. For any spatial eigenfunction of $-\Delta$ with eigenvalue $\lambda\ge0$, the linearized reaction-diffusion mode has matrix $J-\lambda D$. For the continuous rectangular torus, $\lambda=\lambda_k=\sum_j(2\pi k_j/L_j)^2$ with $k\in\mathbb Z^d$. For the periodic grid of [[def-periodic-reaction-diffusion-grid]], the mode indexed by $\ell$ has $\lambda=\lambda_{h,\ell}=4\sum_jh_j^{-2}\sin^2(\pi\ell_j/N_j)$, with $0\le\ell_j<N_j$.

Define
$$
\beta_T=d_2J_{11}+d_1J_{22},\qquad q(\lambda)=\det(J-\lambda D)=d_1d_2\lambda^2-\beta_T\lambda+\det J.
$$
For either domain or grid and each actual mode, $J-\lambda D$ has a positive-real-part eigenvalue exactly when $q(\lambda)<0$; it is Hurwitz exactly when $q(\lambda)>0$, and has a zero eigenvalue when $q(\lambda)=0$. Thus the continuous or discrete linear instability criterion tests the actual corresponding spectrum. If all nonnegative $\lambda$ are regarded as continuously available, then a diffusion-driven unstable band exists exactly when $\beta_T>0$ and $\beta_T^2>4d_1d_2\det J$; its endpoints are
$$
\lambda_\pm=\frac{\beta_T\pm\sqrt{\beta_T^2-4d_1d_2\det J}}{2d_1d_2}.
$$
On a bounded torus or a finite grid, the band criterion alone is not enough: at least one actual Laplacian eigenvalue must lie strictly between $\lambda_-$ and $\lambda_+$.

Let $\mathcal T=(\mathcal K,\mathcal F)$ be a finite TPFA-admissible cell-face mesh from [[def-fv-admissible-cell-face-mesh]] and [[def-tpfa-harmonic-face-scheme]]. Impose homogeneous no-flux boundary conditions: boundary faces contribute zero flux and therefore no conductance. For adjacent cells $K,L$, set
$$
c_{KL}=\sum_{F=K|L}T_F,
$$
where the sum is over their common interior faces and is zero when they are not adjacent. Set $c_{KL}=c_{LK}$ and $m_K=|K|$. If more than one face separates a cell pair, summing their conductances gives the same cell-balance flux as retaining the faces separately. Define the symmetric matrix $L_h$ by $(L_h)_{KK}=\sum_{L\ne K}c_{KL}$ and $(L_h)_{KL}=-c_{KL}$ for $K\ne L$.

For species diffusivities $d_r\ge0$, the no-flux finite-volume diffusion equation is $M U_r'+d_r L_h U_r=0$ for each species $r$, where $M=\operatorname{diag}(|K|)$. Its component equation is
$$
|K|(U_{K,r})'=d_r\sum_{L:c_{KL}>0}c_{KL}(U_{L,r}-U_{K,r}).
$$
The equality is the usual shared-face TPFA balance with outward flux $T_F(U_{K,r}-U_{L,r})$ and no boundary flux. The matrix $L_h$ is symmetric, has zero row sums and nonpositive off-diagonal entries, and obeys $v^{\mathsf T}L_hv=\sum_{\{K,L\}}c_{KL}(v_K-v_L)^2\ge0$, where the sum is over unordered adjacent cell pairs. With $M=\operatorname{diag}(|K|)$, the generator $-M^{-1}L_h$ is self-adjoint in the weighted pairing $\langle v,w\rangle_M=v^{\mathsf T}Mw$. This definition makes no accuracy claim for arbitrary admissible meshes.

**Input:** Either the no-flux TPFA discretization of [[def-fv-tpfa-no-flux-diffusion-specialization]] or the periodic-grid discretization of [[def-periodic-reaction-diffusion-grid]]; a reaction field $F$; a reaction-inward rectangle $R$; coordinate constants $L_i\ge0$ such that $|F_i(z)-F_i(w)|\le L_i|z_i-w_i|$ whenever $z,w\in R$ differ only in coordinate $i$, as required in [[lem-forward-euler-reaction-step-preserves-invariant-rectangle-and-mass]]; $\tau_R=\min_{i:L_i>0}L_i^{-1}$, with $\tau_R=+\infty$ if every $L_i=0$; a state $U^n$ with every cell/node state in $R$; and $0\le\tau\le\tau_R$.

**Procedure:**

1. At every cell/node, compute the forward-Euler reaction value $V_i=U_i^n+\tau F(U_i^n)$.
2. For each species $r$, apply the exact diffusion map $e^{-\tau d_rM^{-1}L_h}$ in the TPFA case or $e^{-\tau d_rA_h^{\rm per}}$ in the periodic-grid case to $(V_{i,r})_i$.
3. Return the resulting state $U^{n+1}$.

This is an approximate reaction substep followed by exact diffusion. The bound $\tau\le\tau_R$ is part of the input contract and is needed for the stated rectangle guarantee; no diffusion CFL restriction is needed because the diffusion map is exact. The procedure makes no claim about finite-precision evaluation of either step.

derivations.claim: On $[0,1]$, $F(0)=F(1)=0$, so the field points inward at both endpoints. Also $|F'(u)|=|r(1-2u)|\le r$, giving the coordinate Lipschitz constant $L=r$ and Euler restriction $\tau\le1/r$.

For $u\in[0,1]$, set $\alpha=\tau r\in[0,1]$. The Euler value is $u^+=u+\alpha u(1-u)\ge0$, while $ 1-u^+=(1-u)(1-\alpha u)\ge0 $ because both factors are nonnegative. Thus the reaction step preserves $[0,1]$.

If $\alpha=\tau r>1$, choose $u$ with $1/\alpha<u<1$. Then $1-u^+=(1-u)(1-\alpha u)<0$, so the Euler map leaves $[0,1]$. Together with step 2.1 this proves the stated necessary-and-sufficient bound for the reaction map.

The reaction map satisfies the hypothesis of [F3] by step 2.1; applying [F2] and then [F3] proves that the full TPFA Lie update also remains in $[0,1]$. For a grid state $U=(u_i)_i$ with positive weights $m_i$, its Euler reaction mass increment is $\sum_i m_i\tau r u_i(1-u_i)$. This is strictly positive for $\tau>0$ exactly when some $u_i\in(0,1)$, and is zero when every $u_i\in\{0,1\}$; for $\tau=0$ it is zero for every state. Thus the mass claim in the Statement holds, and no mass-conservation claim is made.
